subject: Renal
vignette: A 62-year-old woman with small cell lung cancer develops progressive confusion and nausea over 2 days, then has a generalized seizure. Serum sodium is 118 mEq/L with low serum osmolality and inappropriately concentrated urine, consistent with SIADH.
question: Which of the following clinical findings is most characteristic of this electrolyte abnormality?

options.text: Irritability, stupor, and coma without nausea or seizures
Tetany, carpopedal spasm, and a prolonged QT interval
Nausea, malaise, stupor, coma, and seizures
Wide QRS complexes and peaked T waves with muscle weakness
Renal stones, bone pain, abdominal groans, and psychiatric overtones

explanation_correct: Severe hyponatremia lowers extracellular osmolality, so water shifts into brain cells and produces cerebral edema. The classic neurologic spectrum is nausea and malaise progressing to stupor, coma, and seizures. This patient's SIADH from small cell lung cancer causes free-water retention and dilutional hyponatremia. The findings reflect brain dysfunction rather than a peripheral neuromuscular or cardiac conduction problem.

explanation_incorrect.A: Irritability, stupor, and coma are the classic features of hypernatremia, in which neurons shrink; prominent nausea, malaise, and seizures point instead to hyponatremia.
explanation_incorrect.B: Tetany, carpopedal spasm (Trousseau sign), and QT prolongation are features of hypocalcemia from increased neuronal excitability, not of hyponatremia.
explanation_incorrect.D: Wide QRS complexes and peaked T waves with muscle weakness are the ECG and neuromuscular hallmarks of hyperkalemia.
explanation_incorrect.E: Renal stones, bone pain, abdominal groans, and psychiatric overtones are the classic mnemonic for hypercalcemia.

educationalObjective: Severe hyponatremia causes nausea, malaise, stupor, coma, and seizures from cerebral edema, classically due to free-water retention such as SIADH.

subject: Renal
vignette: A 78-year-old man with limited access to water develops weakness and confusion over 3 days. He has been unable to sweat and has had no water intake. Serum sodium is 162 mEq/L and serum osmolality is 340 mOsm/kg. He becomes irritable and later stuporous.
question: Which of the following best characterizes the neurologic manifestations expected from this degree of hypernatremia?

options.text: Irritability, stupor, and coma
Nausea, malaise, and seizures
Tetany, twitching, and a prolonged QT interval
U waves, flattened T waves, and muscle cramps
Decreased deep tendon reflexes, lethargy, and bradycardia

explanation_correct: Hypernatremia raises extracellular osmolality, drawing water out of neurons and causing cerebral shrinkage. This produces irritability, progressing to stupor and coma in severe cases. Unlike hyponatremia, prominent nausea, malaise, and seizures are not the classic presentation. His free-water deficit from ongoing insensible losses explains the high sodium.

explanation_incorrect.B: Nausea, malaise, and seizures characterize hyponatremia, in which water shifts into brain cells and produces cerebral edema rather than neuronal shrinkage.
explanation_incorrect.C: Tetany, twitching (Chvostek sign), and QT prolongation are features of hypocalcemia caused by increased neuronal excitability.
explanation_incorrect.D: U waves, flattened T waves, and muscle cramps are findings of hypokalemia from altered ventricular repolarization.
explanation_incorrect.E: Decreased deep tendon reflexes, lethargy, and bradycardia are features of hypermagnesemia, not hypernatremia.

educationalObjective: Hypernatremia causes neuronal shrinkage with irritability, stupor, and coma, in contrast to the cerebral edema and seizures of hyponatremia.

subject: Renal
vignette: A 54-year-old woman with hypertension takes furosemide 40 mg daily. She reports muscle cramps and progressive weakness. Serum potassium is 2.7 mEq/L, and an ECG is obtained.
question: Which of the following ECG abnormalities is most consistent with her serum potassium level?

options.text: Peaked T waves and widening of the QRS complex
Prolonged QT interval with carpopedal spasm
Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (torsades de pointes)
U waves and flattened T waves
Sinus bradycardia with hypotension and suppressed deep tendon reflexes

explanation_correct: Hypokalemia delays ventricular repolarization, producing flattened T waves and prominent U waves; severe cases cause arrhythmias, muscle cramps, spasm, and weakness. Furosemide increases distal sodium delivery and potassium secretion, a classic cause. The U wave is the signature finding here.

explanation_incorrect.A: Peaked T waves with a widened QRS are the ECG hallmark of hyperkalemia, the opposite potassium disturbance.
explanation_incorrect.B: QT prolongation with carpopedal spasm reflects hypocalcemia and increased neuronal excitability.
explanation_incorrect.C: Torsades de pointes is classically associated with hypomagnesemia (or congenital long QT), not isolated hypokalemia.
explanation_incorrect.E: Bradycardia, hypotension, and reduced reflexes are features of hypermagnesemia from suppressed neuromuscular and cardiac conduction.

educationalObjective: Hypokalemia produces U waves and flattened T waves with cramps and weakness, classically from loop diuretic use.

subject: Renal
vignette: A 68-year-old man with chronic kidney disease (eGFR 18 mL/min/1.73 m²) starts spironolactone for heart failure. One week later he has generalized muscle weakness and palpitations. Serum potassium is 7.2 mEq/L, and ECG shows loss of P waves and QRS widening.
question: Which of the following ECG findings is most characteristic of this patient's electrolyte abnormality?

options.text: U waves with flattened T waves
Peaked (tall, narrow) T waves
Prolonged QT interval with tetany
Torsades de pointes with tetany and hypocalcemia
Sinus bradycardia, hypotension, and decreased deep tendon reflexes

explanation_correct: Hyperkalemia causes progressive ECG changes: peaked T waves first, then PR prolongation and loss of P waves, QRS widening, and ultimately a sine-wave pattern and asystole. Muscle weakness accompanies the conduction abnormality. His potassium-sparing diuretic and reduced renal excretion created a severe hyperkalemia. Peaked T waves are the classic early hallmark.

explanation_incorrect.A: U waves with flattened T waves are the ECG signature of hypokalemia, not hyperkalemia.
explanation_incorrect.C: Prolonged QT interval with tetany is characteristic of hypocalcemia and increased neuronal excitability.
explanation_incorrect.D: Torsades de pointes with tetany and hypocalcemia reflects hypomagnesemia, often when magnesium is below 1.0 mEq/L.
explanation_incorrect.E: Bradycardia, hypotension, and depressed reflexes are features of hypermagnesemia, not hyperkalemia.

educationalObjective: Hyperkalemia produces peaked T waves progressing to wide QRS and loss of P waves, with muscle weakness, especially with potassium-sparing diuretics and renal failure.

subject: Renal
vignette: A 45-year-old woman develops muscle cramps and tingling in her hands and feet 2 days after thyroidectomy. Chvostek and Trousseau signs are positive. Serum calcium is 6.8 mg/dL, and ECG shows QT prolongation.
question: Which of the following best explains her positive Chvostek and Trousseau signs?

options.text: Cerebral edema from water shifting into neurons
Impaired vitamin D activation causing bone pain
Excessive aldosterone causing renal potassium wasting
Hypermagnesemia suppressing neuromuscular transmission
Increased neuronal excitability from low ionized calcium causing tetany and muscle spasm

explanation_correct: Hypocalcemia lowers the threshold for neuronal and muscle depolarization, producing tetany, twitching (Chvostek sign), and carpopedal spasm (Trousseau sign), along with seizures and QT prolongation. Post-thyroidectomy hypoparathyroidism is a classic cause. The positive signs are elicited by triggering latent tetany in an excitability state.

explanation_incorrect.A: Cerebral edema from water shifting into neurons is the mechanism of hyponatremic seizures, not of Chvostek or Trousseau signs.
explanation_incorrect.B: Impaired vitamin D activation contributes to bone disease and hypocalcemia but does not directly produce the acute tetany of a positive Chvostek sign.
explanation_incorrect.C: Aldosterone excess causes hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis, not the neuromuscular irritability of hypocalcemia.
explanation_incorrect.D: Hypermagnesemia suppresses neuromuscular transmission and reduces reflexes, producing the opposite of tetany.

educationalObjective: Hypocalcemia causes tetany, seizures, QT prolongation, and positive Chvostek/Trousseau signs from increased neuronal excitability.

subject: Renal
vignette: A 66-year-old man with multiple myeloma presents with constipation, abdominal pain, polyuria, and bone pain. Serum calcium is 14.2 mg/dL. He is anxious and mildly confused.
question: Which of the following mnemonics best summarizes the classic clinical manifestations of this patient's electrolyte abnormality?

options.text: Stones, bones, groans, thrones, and psychiatric overtones
Tetany, seizures, Chvostek sign, and QT prolongation
Nausea, malaise, stupor, coma, and seizures
U waves, flattened T waves, and muscle weakness
Bone loss, osteomalacia, and rickets

explanation_correct: Hypercalcemia classically presents with renal stones, bone pain, abdominal groans, increased urinary frequency (thrones), and psychiatric overtones such as anxiety and altered mental status. Malignancy with bone destruction, as in multiple myeloma, is a common cause. The mnemonic captures the multiorgan effects of elevated calcium.

explanation_incorrect.B: Tetany, seizures, Chvostek sign, and QT prolongation are features of hypocalcemia, the opposite disturbance.
explanation_incorrect.C: Nausea, malaise, stupor, coma, and seizures are the neurologic spectrum of severe hyponatremia.
explanation_incorrect.D: U waves, flattened T waves, and muscle weakness are findings of hypokalemia.
explanation_incorrect.E: Bone loss, osteomalacia in adults, and rickets in children are consequences of hypophosphatemia.

educationalObjective: Hypercalcemia presents with stones, bones, groans, thrones, and psychiatric overtones, commonly from malignancy or bone destruction.

subject: Renal
vignette: A 58-year-old woman with chronic diarrhea and poor nutrition has a serum magnesium of 0.7 mEq/L. She develops tetany and episodes of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia. Potassium is 3.1 mEq/L and calcium is 7.6 mg/dL.
question: Which of the following best explains the coexistence of her low potassium and low calcium?

options.text: Hypermagnesemia suppresses parathyroid hormone and aldosterone, lowering calcium and potassium
Hyperphosphatemia causes metastatic calcifications and renal potassium wasting
Hypophosphatemia causes osteomalacia and impaired renal potassium conservation
Hypomagnesemia impairs PTH secretion and renal potassium conservation, causing hypocalcemia and hypokalemia
Hypercalcemia suppresses PTH and causes renal potassium wasting

explanation_correct: Hypomagnesemia, especially below 1.0 mEq/L, causes hypocalcemia by impairing parathyroid hormone secretion and producing PTH resistance, and causes hypokalemia by increasing renal potassium wasting. It also produces tetany and torsades de pointes, as in this patient. Correcting the magnesium is required before the potassium and calcium abnormalities can be fully corrected.

explanation_incorrect.A: Hypermagnesemia causes decreased deep tendon reflexes, lethargy, bradycardia, hypotension, and cardiac arrest, not the tetany and hypokalemia seen here.
explanation_incorrect.B: Hyperphosphatemia causes renal stones, metastatic calcifications, and hypocalcemia, but it is not the primary driver of renal potassium wasting in this vignette.
explanation_incorrect.C: Hypophosphatemia causes bone loss, osteomalacia, and rickets rather than the tetany and torsades described.
explanation_incorrect.E: Hypercalcemia produces stones, bones, groans, thrones, and psychiatric overtones, not combined hypocalcemia and hypokalemia.

educationalObjective: Hypomagnesemia below 1.0 mEq/L causes tetany, torsades, hypokalemia, and hypocalcemia through impaired PTH secretion and renal potassium wasting.
